title: Thioglycollate Broth

references.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

purpose: A general-purpose enrichment broth used to cultivate a broad range of organisms including obligate anaerobes, microaerophiles, and facultative anaerobes in a single tube, and commonly used as a sterility-test medium.

reference.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

compositionPerLiter.ingredient: Agar (small amount to reduce convection currents)

reference.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

preparationSummary: Suspend the dehydrated powder in distilled/deionized water, heat to dissolve, dispense into tubes, and sterilize; the sodium thioglycollate and small agar content create an oxygen gradient down the tube, with the resazurin indicator turning pink in the aerated upper zone to visually mark it.

sterilization.value: commonly autoclaved at 121°C for 15 minutes for typical batch volumes
sterilization.dependsOn: batch volume, container, and autoclave validation — not a universal setting for every load

reference.label: Difco & BBL Manual of Microbiological Culture Media

storage: Store prepared tubes at room temperature protected from light; reheat (steam or boiling water bath) to drive off absorbed oxygen if the top has turned pink from prolonged storage before use.

shelfLife.value: manufacturer-stated shelf life varies by product and storage condition

expectedAppearance: Clear to slightly opalescent broth with a faint pink zone only in the uppermost aerated portion of an unused tube; the rest of the tube should be colorless to pale.
qualityControl: Confirm sterility of an uninoculated control tube and check that the oxygen-gradient indicator zone appears only near the surface before use in critical work.

reactions.reaction: Growth concentrated in the lower (low-oxygen) portion of the tube
Growth concentrated near the surface (high-oxygen) portion of the tube

manufacturerNotes: Growth pattern along the tube (surface vs. bottom vs. throughout) gives a rough indication of an organism's oxygen requirement, though it is not a substitute for a dedicated anaerobic identification workflow.
